title: Fall Back! Daylight Saving Time Ends on November 1
summary:
Good news: on Sunday, November 1, 2026, millions of people in North America get a bonus hour. Clocks go back by one hour, ending Daylight Saving Time (DST) for this year and returning an extra 60 minutes to the weekend.

The switch also moves more sunlight into the morning, which should make it a little easier to wake up for school or work during the shorter winter days ahead. DST began this year on March 8.

Why do we do this at all? The idea started during World War I. In 1916, the German Empire moved clocks forward to cut artificial lighting and save fuel, and the United States and Britain copied the trick. Countries returned to standard time after the war, then brought DST back for World War II.

Then came the messy part. After 1945, the US let states and districts pick their own dates, creating a confusing patchwork — by 1965, Iowa alone had 23 different sets of start and end dates! The Uniform Time Act of 1966 set one national schedule, though Hawaii, most of Arizona and several US territories chose not to take part.

Since 2007, DST has run from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. About 70 countries observe some form of it, though experts say the twice-yearly change can disrupt sleep and concentration.

Some US states want to stay on DST all year, but that needs federal approval. The Sunshine Protection Act would make DST permanent; the House passed it in July 2026 by 308 votes to 117, but the Senate has not approved it yet. Until then: fall back, and enjoy the extra hour.
why_it_matters: Clock changes affect sleep, school and work for millions of people twice a year, and the debate over making Daylight Saving Time permanent would change daily routines across the whole country.

questions.question: What is the Sunshine Protection Act?

background_read: Daylight Saving Time is a system of moving the clocks forward by one hour for part of the year, so that the evening stays light for longer.
It began as a way to save fuel: with more daylight in the evening, people needed less artificial lighting.
When the clocks go back in autumn, places return to standard time, and the morning becomes lighter instead.
Because changing the clocks twice a year can disrupt sleep and cause confusion, some people want to stop the switches and stay on one time all year, but that change needs federal approval.
